section_title: What wisdom had the rulers failed to recognize?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 6 Among the mature, however, we speak a message of wisdom—but not the wisdom of this age or of the rulers of this age, who are coming to nothing. 7 No, we speak of the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God, which He destined for our glory before time began. 8 None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory. 9 Rather, as it is written: “No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.”

context_lines: Paul does speak wisdom, but it is different from the wisdom associated with the present age and its passing rulers. The word translated mature is teleios (TEH-lay-oss), τέλειος. [Thayer’s entry](https://biblehub.com/greek/5046.htm) includes full-grown or mature and applies it here in contrast with infants in Christ. Paul is describing growth in understanding, rather than a secret class of believers who no longer need correction.

God’s wisdom was hidden and destined for His people’s glory before time began. The rulers failed to recognize it and crucified the Lord of glory. Their judgment about Jesus did not reveal the true value of the One they rejected.

Paul then draws on [Isaiah 64:4](https://biblehub.com/bsb/isaiah/64.htm), which speaks of the God who acts for those who wait for Him. The next verse is essential to Paul’s point: God has revealed these things by His Spirit. This is not simply a statement that nothing God has prepared can ever be known.
common_interpretation_lines: Christians commonly understand this as God’s saving wisdom being hidden from the world’s rulers and made known through the Spirit. Readers differ over the scope of the rulers: [Wesley’s notes on verses 6–8](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-st-pauls-first-epistle-to-the-corinthians/) discuss Jewish and Gentile rulers, while the [USCCB note on verse 8](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/1corinthians/2) sees human rulers with spiritual powers behind them. Both readings recognize the crucifixion as a failure to understand who Christ is.
god_plan_lines: [Acts 4:27–28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/acts/4.htm) names Herod, Pilate, Gentiles and people of Israel in the opposition to Jesus, while placing what happened within God’s purpose. Human rejection did not take Him outside God’s saving plan.

Jesus’ own explanation in [Luke 24:26–27, 44–47](https://biblehub.com/bsb/luke/24.htm) connects His suffering with glory, resurrection and the worldwide proclamation of forgiveness. Paul’s contrast between the rejected Lord and God’s hidden wisdom belongs within that larger story.
